content: Uranium-238 (U-238) is the most abundant isotope of uranium found in nature. It undergoes a decay process over a very long timescale, with a half-life of approximately 4.46 billion years. Depleted uranium primarily consists of U-238, while enriched uranium contains a higher proportion of the fissile isotope uranium-235 (U-235). Reprocessed uranium is also predominantly U-238 but includes significant amounts of uranium-236 (U-236) and other isotopes ranging from uranium-232 to uranium-238, excluding uranium-237. Nuclear Energy Applications In nuclear reactors, uranium-238 can be converted into plutonium-239 (Pu-239) through a process called breeding. Plutonium-239 can then be used as a fuel source or in nuclear weapons. In a typical nuclear reactor, up to one-third of the energy generated comes from the fission of plutonium-239, which is produced in situ from uranium-238 rather than being supplied as a fuel. Breeder Reactors Uranium-238 cannot be directly used as nuclear fuel but serves as a fertile material to produce fissile plutonium-239. Breeder reactors are designed to facilitate this transmutation process, converting uranium-238 into plutonium-239. Estimates suggest that there is enough uranium-238 to sustain breeder reactors for anywhere between 10,000 years and 5 billion years. As of December 2005, the BN-600 reactor at the Beloyarsk Nuclear Power Station in Russia was the only operational breeder reactor producing power. Russia has plans to construct another unit, the BN-800, at the same site. Japan's Monju breeder reactor is also planned for restart, and both China and India have announced intentions to develop breeder reactors. Additionally, the Clean And Environmentally Safe Advanced Reactor (CAESAR) concept, which uses steam as a moderator, is being developed to potentially utilize uranium-238 as fuel after being initiated with low-enriched uranium (LEU). However, this design remains in its early stages of development. Radiation Shielding Uranium-238 is also employed as a material for radiation shielding. Its alpha radiation is easily contained by the non-radioactive casing of the shielding, and its high atomic weight and electron density make it highly effective at absorbing gamma rays and X-rays. However, it is less effective than water at stopping fast neutrons. Both metallic depleted uranium and depleted uranium dioxide are used as shielding materials. Uranium is approximately five times more effective than lead as a gamma-ray shield, allowing for thinner shielding layers with equivalent effectiveness. DUCRETE, a concrete material incorporating uranium dioxide aggregate instead of gravel, is being explored for use in dry cask storage systems for radioactive waste. Downblending Downblending is the process of diluting highly enriched uranium (HEU) with depleted or natural uranium to produce low-enriched uranium (LEU) suitable for use in commercial nuclear fuel. Uranium-238 from depleted or natural uranium is also combined with recycled plutonium from weapons stockpiles to create mixed oxide (MOX) fuel, which is being redirected for use as reactor fuel. This dilution process ensures that any nation or group acquiring the finished fuel would need to undertake the costly and complex enrichment and separation processes again before assembling a weapon. Nuclear Weapons Modern nuclear weapons often use uranium-238 as a tamper material. The tamper surrounds the fissile core, reflecting neutrons and adding inertia to the compression of the plutonium charge, thereby increasing the weapon's efficiency and reducing the amount of fissile material required. In thermonuclear weapons, uranium-238 can encase the fusion fuel. The high flux of energetic neutrons from the fusion reaction induces fission in the uranium-238, significantly increasing the weapon's yield. These weapons are known as fission-fusion-fission devices, as the explosion involves three consecutive stages. A large portion of the explosive yield in such designs comes from the final fission stage fueled by uranium-238, producing vast amounts of radioactive fission products. For example, in the 1952 Ivy Mike thermonuclear test, 4 megatons of the total yield were attributed to the fast fission of the depleted uranium tamper. Depleted uranium, having no critical mass, can be added to thermonuclear bombs in nearly unlimited quantities. The 1961 Soviet Tsar Bomba test yielded 50 megatons, with over 90% of the energy coming from fusion, as the uranium-238 final stage was replaced with lead. Had uranium-238 been used, the yield could have reached 100 megatons, producing fallout equivalent to one-third of the global total at that time. Radioactivity and Decay Uranium-238 decays into thorium-234, which has a half-life of 246,000 years. This property makes it useful for dating sediments between 100,000 and 1,200,000 years old. One mole of uranium-238 emits approximately 3 million alpha particles per second, producing an equal number of thorium-234 atoms. In a closed system, equilibrium is reached, with all decay products except lead-206 and uranium-238 present in fixed ratios, though in slowly decreasing amounts. The amount of lead-206 increases as uranium-238 decreases. Each step in the decay chain occurs at the same rate of 3 million decays per second per mole of uranium-238. In equilibrium, the amount of each decay product, except the final product lead, is proportional to its half-life. Starting with pure uranium-238, equilibrium is achieved for the first three steps in the decay chain within a human timescale. The decay of uranium-238 releases energy at a rate of approximately 3 microwatts per mole.
